Content: I'm not sure yet how I feel about these paint pens. I am a painter and paint with oils, acrylics, watercolors and I draw with all sorts of pencils and pens. These paint pens are fun to use but there are a couple of things I don't like about them. When filling in a drawing say for example a lady's skirt, the paint doesn't fill in the area on the first try. It's because the pen tips are fine which is nice for smaller areas but not so much for larger areas. This is another issue. Filling in smaller areas, the pens flood the paper and the paint goes over the outlines of the sketch.It's similar to painting with watercolor paints. Many times the paint will seep over the sketched lines. This is fine for a watercolor painting but not for the images I am working on right now.I am creating Christmas cards and I want the paint to be nice and neat and filled in with no 'holidays'.I do like the colors and the pen nibs are nice and firm.It will take some practice I suppose to get to where I want to be with these paint pens. Like I said, they ARE fun to use.Update June 20:I need to make a correction on the red color selection. There are two reds. I accidentally mixed the darker red pen with the metallic pens. So the darker red pen is a nice shade of red but the second red pen looks like a dark pink. or lighter red which is simply dark pink.Keep your pens separate! Lol.Update June 25I discovered that if you use a dampened paint brush and brush over your pen painted area quickly, the brush will smooth out the paint and make it go further. I just did it after drawing a holly leaf with the darker green pen.Because the paint in the pens is acrylic you can brush it. Use a good brush though and be careful when painting along the lines. I'm glad I now know I can brush this paint (not being very experienced with these pens) because when using the paint pens on a large area they have a tendency to leave line marks and 'holidays'. A brush takes care of all of that. The metallic paint pens are really bad about this. They leave scratch marks, line marks and holidays and going back over the painted area just creates a mess. The pens tend to flood and this leaves weird looking spots on your picture.Unless you are experienced and skillful with a paint brush I advise you to practice on a scrap piece of paper before applying this to your finished picture.

Content: Shipping was so fast! These are great for writing on glass. I have a lot of experience working with Pebeo brand - the most well-known of glass and ceramic paints. These are just as good, if not better - at a FRACTION of the price! Colors are vibrant and don't alter when baking. The paint flow is consistent which avoids "oops - it pooped" mistakes that can ruin a project (and cause tons of frustration.) I would include a photo of my projects, but the second they were cooled the recipients ran off with them. (They surprised me by arriving while the jars were in the oven.) No one could believe they were handmade - and I finished the large project happily, with lots of paint left for another day. I highly recommend these and will order more when these are gone. Only one request from Zeyar: more colors, please! I would buy them all!** IMPORTANT TIP **: When you put your glass project in the oven it is VERY IMPORTANT to PLACE GLASS IN A COLD OVEN. Place the glass inside, turn it on, bake. LEAVE GLASS IN OVEN UNTIL COOL. Once oven is again cold, you can safely remove the glass. This should be in Zeyars instructions but isn't. If you don't do this the glass can shock, and that's not only bad for your project but downright dangerous. Anyone who works with glass knows this but if you're new, you may not. This will avoid shattered glass, and it also won't crack while cooling.

Content: To make the color permanent, you have to let the project dry for hours, then bake it at 400 degrees for a half hour and let it cool in the oven for another half hour. So items that melt or that are too big for the oven won’t achieve permanence. It’s nice that the instructions for getting the ink to flow are written on each marker, on the box and on an enclosed card, all with drawings to illustrate. The drawings show that you shake it not from top to bottom but like you’re shaking down an old-fashioned thermometer to remove the last reading. It would be nice if the ink color was also written on each marker. Hard to tell some of them apart. Black and brown are almost the same, and red is nearly indistinguishable from the fuscia, which has a purply pink cap. Interesting that you have to push the tip to one side to kind of burp it, before pumping the point on scrap paper until ink comes down to cover the tip and starts to pool. The instructions say to practice on scrap, then reactivate and apply to your project. When the flow gets thin, repeat the process from the thermometer shake. I found this made for uneven application.In my set of 12  colors, there was too little difference between the colors. Instead of a fuscia and red that almost match, for example, I could have used a second green. They’re ingenious little devices, though, and I plan to personalize mugs and stemware.

Content: These water-based Flymax Paint Markers are very vibrant on coated black papers and on top of lines made by alcohol-based markers (and other writing utensils)! I am extremely grateful for these markers, which are easy to control when illustrating small artwork. They work exactly as described when the directions on the back of the box are followed! I have added extra details to the box directions to help with anyone having trouble, especially when the pen is being used for the first time:1. Leave the pen cap on and shake the pen several times prior to using.2. Uncap, and press down on the pen tip (onto some paper) with enough force to push the tip inside of the pen. Release pressure to let the tip back out. Please do this several times to encourage the white ink to come out until the white ink flows when you write with the tip.3. Recap the pen tightly after using.If you are using a thicker substrate to write with (like ballpoint pen ink, which is actually a paste made by dissolving dye in solvent), the white Paint Marker water-based ink might sink through the thick ink a bit and show some of the color underneath. If you are drawing on top of alcohol-based markers or watercolors, the white Paint Marker may show up better since markers and diluted paints usually sink deeply into textured paper and don't leave a thick substrate on top of the paper. Happy drawing/writing/decorating! :D

No way, José.Extra Fine lines are simply impossible with this marker, and it is too expensive for Amazon, if I return an $11 product. I don't want to lose my return privileges by being deemed an over-user of that privilege.This marker is worthless for its advertised purpose, but good for others. Content: We have a group of stained glass artists who share a facility where we live, and have had difficulty finding a way to mark patterns on dark glass.  Our usual black felt tip markers just become invisible.  Our various white markers had lines too thick - the main problem, were too faint, or did not work consistently - extremely frustrating.  Often it was more than one of these issues.  But these wonderful pens solve that problem.Pros: Very nice thin line, paint flow starts quickly and stays flowing evenly - no blobs, and smears.  If it does stop, just a quick push down on the tip restarts it.  We do recommend it be stored with the tip either down or on it's side.  If used for stained glass, the lubricant from the grinder does not wash away the paint!Con: Almost none with exception that you need to give it time for the paint to dry - usually 10-15 minutes or so.  A heat gun might speed this up.  Also, for stained glass work, the grinder can start to chip off if grinding right next to the paint line.Overall the pros greatly outweigh the minor cons in our view.

Content: These water-based acrylic paint markers are a good alternative to oil-based markers. You’ll still have to shake them and press the tip to activate, just as you would with oil-based paint markers. The advantage over oil-based is that the paint goes on smoothly with no clumps, and the coverage is very good. These work on light or dark paper with full coverage. Colors can be layered once dry.I like to use oil-based paint markers to draw or write on plastic surfaces and was hoping these would work just as well. They’re a decent alternative but they do bead up on very slick or glossy surfaces. However, the paint will stay on once dry if it is something that won’t be handled often. But if the plastic has any tooth or texture, these work very well. The paint also beaded up a little on glass, though not as much as on the slick plastic surfaces. I tried them on metal, rocks, wood, craft foam, and fabric, all with success. They also are wonderfully and highly metallic colors, shimmering beautifully with the slightest amount of light. They are easy to manipulate to get a variety of marks and line variation. I’m happy that it’s a more kid-friendly alternative to oil-based markers (although still with supervision).

Content: Got these for my wife, who really enjoys art supplies.She found the colors from these markers to be disappointingly dull. Unlike other reviewers who have called them brilliant, she says to her most of them looked like variations of brown, especially when used on white fabric instead of paper. They can certainly be good for a decorative project.We didn’t think they were great on paper. Since they contain acrylic paints and not watercolors, they require heavier paper. The tips are blunt and made of fabric with some fibers that came loose while my wife was testing the marker.All is not negative. On the plus side, they worked really well and looked great on rock (also in the picture). If you have a bunch of rocks to decorate, these markers are for you. Otherwise, we’re not recommending them.

Content:
I bought these for fun to use on both paper and rocks. I love them! They release ink smoothly on either smooth or rough surfaces and the metallics are truly shiny without being garish or cheap looking. The colors are vibrant and saturated, but still pair well with the matte colors from other pen sets—it gives a sheen to the same colors instead of popping/taking all of the attention, which I really like!

For anyone just getting started with rock painting and not sure what size to get: I bought the 2-3mm size and it’s great for filling in larger sections while still allowing me to attempt some details, like highlights. It’s not overly wide or particularly fine; it’s a good “medium” size. Since it’s harder to control for fine details though, I would recommend also getting some fine pens (like 0.7mm) for detailed drawings, in addition to this 2-3mm size for filling in sections or backgrounds. You’d likely only need a pen wider than this 2-3mm for larger scale artwork, as this is plenty big enough for rock painting.

My only complaint about this particular set of pens is that I wish it came with a white pen too (maybe pearl or iridescent for the shine). Otherwise I’m very happy with it! Been using it for a couple of months and no clogging or drying out so far. If you’re debating between the smaller or larger set of the 2-3mm pens, get the one with more pens. It’ll be worth it to have more color options!

I recommend this set for quality but inexpensive paint pens, and plan to buy them again when my current set gets used up. They’d make a good gift, too!

The colors are not totally opaque over black, but no worse than name brands, and I was especially happy with the opacity of white and black. Silver is totally opaque. The only downsides are that there was some unexpected color lift when I tested light colors over what I thought was dry black, and I don’t expect these pens hold a ton of paint. Content: I bought these specifically for coloring wax seals but with the dual purpose of card making calligraphy if that didn't work out. It comes with a decent selection of colors and the pens are double ended with a nub and a brush head.I tried them on some junk mail when they arrived and was happy with the smooth flow of the brush head. The white in particular stood out quite well, which is usually the most disappointing color in my experience. It takes a few seconds to dry so you have to keep that in mind.As far as using on the wax seals, it kind of worked, but not well. The paint spread and slipped across the wax and neither head was particularly effective. The brush head was a bit too thick and bled. The result is not something I would be happy gifting, so that's out the window.My second test was on card stock. This was better. I prefer the brush head and they glide well but were varying thickness. The nubs seem more consistent and offer a bolder line. My biggest complaint here is that almost every single color is flat matte. Out of the few I tested, only the gold had a metallic hue. This really depends on your needs, but for me, it's not the prettiest effect for card making. Will probably work best on rocks and maybe glass if it doesn't spread too much before drying.The other drawback is the flimsy box. Couldn't get the markers back in and you have to store these flat (horizontally) to prevent leakage. So provided I decide to keep these, I have to figure out how to store them properly. Hope this helps someone make their decision!

Content: I recently had the pleasure of trying out the 24 Colors Acrylic Paint Pens, and I must say, they exceeded my expectations. These dual-tip pens are perfect for a wide range of art projects, including rock painting, ceramic decoration, woodcraft, plastic art, calligraphy, scrapbooking, brush lettering, card making, and DIY crafts.One of the standout features of these paint pens is their water resistance. The medium tip is perfect for filling in larger areas or creating bold lines, while the brush tip offers more flexibility for detailed work or brush lettering. The dual-tip design provides versatility and convenience, eliminating the need for multiple pens or brushes.The size of the pens is just right, fitting comfortably in my hand and allowing for easy maneuverability. The barrels are sturdy and durable, ensuring that the pens will last through multiple projects without any issues. The vibrant and rich colors of the paint are a delight to work with, adding a pop of life to any artwork.Overall, I highly recommend the 24 Colors Acrylic Paint Pens for anyone looking for a reliable and versatile set of paint pens. Their water resistance, lack of leakage, smooth flow, and convenient dual-tip design make them a must-have for artists of all levels. Whether you're a professional artist or a hobbyist, these pens will surely elevate your art projects to the next level.

Content: My backyard has a bunch of rocks.  Every time I do my yard, I end up with at least a bucket of rocks varying in different shapes and sizes.I decided to start my own rock garden and had the opportunity to give these a try.  These come with a large variety of colors and what's great is that the tips were not getting worn on the rocks, which was great as well.  I decided to go against putting a base coat on these to save on time and was surprised that even without a base coat the color was able to still pop through.  Depending on how perfect you want your rocks, I do recommend putting a coat of base coat though.  As for the lighter colors, you do have to go through another pass after drying as the dark color of the rocks do appear to show through.  After you are done, I do recommend not skipping the clear coat though.  That will help seal in the color and even add some shine.The use is just like any other paint marker.  You shake it up a few times and then compress the tip on a piece of paper or surface to prime the tip with paint.As mentioned, no issues with the color and could see you using these to even customize stickers; however, it took forever to get here.  I think it was about a month before I got the markers.  Not sure what the hold up was, but when it was out for delivery, it didn't make it until 2 days later.  Also, because of the variety of colors, I would have wished for each color to be marked what the color was as a lot look very similar.

Content: Our family has had a generally positive experience with the Funcils 5 Acrylic Black Paint Pen set. These versatile pens have proven to be quite useful for a variety of creative projects that we engage in together. The assortment of tip sizes – ranging from 1mm to 15mm – has allowed us to explore different techniques on a variety of surfaces, including plastic, canvas, wood, and even glass.The fine tip options were particularly handy for intricate detailing, while the jumbo pens were perfect for broader strokes and bolder designs. This variety made the set a go-to tool for family crafting sessions, where each of us could find the right pen for our respective projects.The ink quality is generally good, providing rich and consistent coverage across different surfaces. However, we did notice one minor drawback that led to a 4-star rating. The issue revolves around the ink flow control. It appears that there can be an excess of ink on the nib when starting to use the pen, which can result in a messy application if not carefully managed. We found that pressing down the nib to help the ink flow actually caused the opposite problem – an overflow of ink that quickly made our designs messy.This isn't a dealbreaker for us, as we've learned to delicately control the flow by wiping the nib before use. It's a small inconvenience, but it's worth mentioning for those who might be new to using paint pens. Once we got the hang of managing the ink flow, the pens performed admirably and allowed us to bring our creative visions to life.All in all, the Funcils 5 Acrylic Black Paint Pen set has earned its place in our family's creative toolkit. The range of tip sizes and the ability to work on various surfaces make it a versatile choice for our crafty endeavors. While the issue of ink flow control does exist, it's manageable with a little practice, and the results are definitely worth the effort. If you're looking for a set of paint pens to spark your family's artistic side, this one is definitely worth considering.

Content: I was lucky enough to be able to test three different Funcils sets at the same time (gold, silver, and black).  Many acrylic pens require constant shaking to maintain paint flow, but these have no such issues.  They take some time to prime but, once that’s done, the paint flows very smoothly.  If anything, it may be a little too fluid for some tasks.  It’s runnier than others I’ve used and a lot can come out at once, which means longer drying times (10+ minutes in some cases).Once fully dry, it has a nice semi-gloss finish that feels very durable.  The drying characteristics often depend on the material you’re drawing on, however.  I found these worked well on watercolour paper and canvas but, when used on smooth surfaces like plastic or glass, they have a tendency to rub off.  I think they’re best suited to porous materials like fabric, canvas, wood, or stone.The different Funcils colours generally mark well on each other (please see photo...and try not to notice that I managed to write one entire section upside down).  The silver and gold stand out nicely on the black (and vice versa), but I found they don’t cover over darker colours quite so well.  They’re often streaky and need at least two coats to achieve a good opaque layer.  The semi-gloss finish might also make it harder for other paints to adhere, so these may not be the best choice for a base layer.I really liked the variety of different nibs.  The fine nibs (1 and 3 mm) are great for detail work, but the markers are so similar in size/shape that I often grab one thinking it's the other.  The 3 and 6 mm nibs are reversible (bullet and chisel tips), and the 15 mm nib has a unique flattened chisel tip with three flat surfaces.The only major concern I have is longevity.  They don’t seem prone to drying out, but I’ve only been using them for three days, so it’s hard to reach a full conclusion in that time frame.  I also worry that, since they tend to put a lot of paint out at once, they’ll run out faster than other pens.  Only time will tell in either regard.At $15.95, I think these are well-priced for the quality and variety they offer.  Most comparable sets only have one or two pen sizes, but these are well-suited to a range of applications.  The paint itself has a couple of minor issues but, from what I’ve seen so far, I’d certainly recommend them.My rating: 4.5 stars

Content: We've used Funcil chalk markers so we were interested to try out these black acrylic markers.They have to be activated (easy enough) like most paint markers, and once that's done they can be quite juicy, especially the larger, chisel tip ones. If any of the pens start to run a bit dry then you press the nibs down on paper (or whatever surface) a few times and then they run again smoothly.Ink flow in general is good and things can get a bit messy with the larger tips, but the ink washes off your hands pretty easily.The variety of tip types (point and chisel) and sizes (1mm to 15mm) covers all bases, though you would really need to be working on larger or rougher, more porous surfaces to get the best out of (or need) the larger pens.I only tried them out on rocks and they covered the surfaces well with the ink providing a smooth and fairly glossy surface on smoother rocks. They worked well with stones and pebbles and also in covering a stone that already had a layer of acrylic paint on it. I have used the finest tipped pen of this set before (it came with a Funcil watercolour set) and I find it to be fine enough for most detailed line work. The larger pens are of less use to me, but would come into their own on larger images/surfaces and rougher material i.e. wood.Value-wise it is a good price compared with, for example, Uni Posca's etc., but only if you want all of these sizes, whereas I would prefer a set that comprised only the three smallest sizes for less money, or provided a variety of different colours.I haven't used Uni Posca or Molotow markers, but based on this performance these would seem to be decent budget options to consider. The question that remains therefore is do you need a set with all these sizes in one colour or would your needs be better met by a multi-colour set or individual pens?

Content: Soy una persona muy creativa, a la que le gusta probar todo tipo de manualidades y descubrir material nuevo con el crear. En especial, me gusta probar sobre diferentes superficies a las tradicionales y este tipo de rotuladores con pintura acrílica son ideales.Este pack de rotuladores está formado por 5 unidades de diferente grosor, todos ellos en color negro. Hay tres con puntas redondeadas más finas y tienen un grosor de 1 mm, luego va uno de 3 mm, seguido de uno de 5 mm. Los otros dos tienen una punta ancha que abarca más superficie y son de 10 y 15 mm de ancho, aunque también se pueden usar por la punta e ir variando el grosor. Esto último es muy útil para lettering o caligrafía oriental, ya que permite más versatilidad.En la propia caja indica el funcionamiento con imágenes y un pequeño texto en inglés. Pero se resume en agitar los rotuladores hasta que suene la bola y mantener la agitación unos segundos. Luego apretar la punta contra la superficie varias veces hasta que baje la tinta. Si es la primera vez, mejor hacerlo varias veces y apretar con los dedos la punta para hacer que la almohadilla haga bajar la tinta con más facilidad. Recomiendo realizar esto en un folio aparte, ya que al principio puede salir más tinta de la deseada y hacer pruebas hasta que le pilles el truquillo al rotulador.Tal y como he dicho, se puede usar en todo tipo de superficies: papel, cartón, madera, metal, cristal, piedra, plástico, arcilla, etc. Eso sí, según el material requerirá darle otra pasada, aunque de una pasada cubre la superficie. En mi caso, he hecho una creación con corcho, ya que es una superficie porosa y oscura, y de una pasada la ha recubierto toda. He usado los 5 rotuladores diferentes y no se nota el cambio entre uno u otro al pintar, queda totalmente uniforme. Eso sí, con los gruesos sale más pintura y eso hace que requiera esperar un rato hasta que se seque por completo. Para evitar que se deteriore la creación es recomendable usar un spray de barniz al agua para pintura acrílica (existen en acabado mate o brillante) para preservar la pintura y poder usar las creaciones en el exterior.Los rotuladores vienen en una caja circular muy divertida, ya que vienen una especie de monstruos que si vas girando la caja puedes hacer diferentes combinaciones entre las caras. También es un buen packaging, por qué puedes usarlos en una de las dos partes de la caja. Se puede cerrar bien sin que se abra la caja y poderla llevar a todas partes. Está hecha en cartón, lo cual es sostenible y no incorpora plásticos.Estaría genial que Funcils sacara packs así con otros colores, como blanco, ya que con sólo el negro pueden quedar un poco pobres las creaciones. Aunque existen también en dorado y plateado y combinados con este se pueden hacer ideas muy creativas y llamativas.

Content: As with a lot of paint markers, these have strengths and weaknesses.The five pens come in a funky cardboard tube. The two largest ones are wrapped in plastic, which must be removed. All of the pens have a ball bearing mixer inside, so they have to be shaken before use. The instructions say to pump the nib 2-3 times to get the ink flowing. That's true of the smaller pens, but I found the two largest markers needed their nibs pumped quite a few times to get the ink flowing well. Once primed, all of the pens flow really well. Ink laydown is consistent and smooth.I tested the pens on paper first and found them to be really nice to use. They produce a very rich, opaque black with virtually no bleed. With the larger markers, you will notice come cockling of the paper, just as if you were using acrylic paint, so I would advise using at least 300gsm paper or card if you plan to use the chunkier markers for drawing and illustration.Using the pens on other surfaces had mixed results. On anything porous, the ink adheres well. However, on shiny or hard surfaces, I did notice some beading, and the ink adhesion wasn't great on anything glossy. It could be easily scratched off glass, plastic and metal, so if you did use the ink on those surfaces, you'd need to varnish afterwards to protect it.Given their relatively low cost, I think these are decent paint markers. If you're looking to draw on hard surfaces specifically, then you might want to look elsewhere, but if used on paper, card and porous surfaces, they perform really well and are a good buy.

Content: My wife started rock painting before we were married. And then took off many years to start a family and focus on the home among other things. Over the past year, she has returned to the hobby.In the beginning, when she restarted, she tried acrylic paint pens with less than satisfactory results. We tried the recommended brands, but she had issues with how well the paint covered the surfaces, issues with the tips, specifically with fine detail and also failures of the pens which resulted in leaks and drips. She eventually, settled on using brushes instead of pens. But, in the back of her mind, she hadn't given up on the convenience of using the pens.Recently we came across this offering which was very economically priced and seemed to promise better performance. So, we placed our order.The set contains 24 colors. The pens are double ended which saves money buying two of each. Although we'd have to say neither is particularly sharp. So, detailed work is still an open issue.What these pens supply is really good coverage on the first coat. And superfast drying times - within minutes on smooth rock. Right now, they are new so we can't really judge if the points are going to hold up but, for now we don't have any drips or leaks.So, it seems we may have an alternative to brushes for the broader areas of a surface. But for the details it seems brushes are still her go to tool. We'll have to keep looking for the right pen.So, these are economically price pens that provide very good, first coat coverage that dries relatively quickly. The pens come in a good variety of colors and the tips seem to be holding up well so far. At least as good as anything we've seen including the tips we've seen on the more expensive brands. If you've been looking for an inexpensive brand of capable acrylic pens, you may want to consider giving these one's a try.

Content: We love paint markers in this house!  I have a lot of grandkids, and when they come over, they almost always want to do a craft project.  As you might imagine, paint markers can come in very handy for crafting.  This set of 24 markers is very nice.  I tried out the colors using both the ball-tip and paintbrush tip.  The color feeds beautifully, without any kind of priming, which is often a feature of paint markers.  I love the pretty, vibrant colors, though I do agree that a true red, and a true kelly green would be nice.  But for most purposes, the slightly off-colored green and red are just fine.  None of the grandkids have mentioned this at all, so I'm definitely quibbling.  The markers came in a flimsy cardboard box, without any kind of separation.  So if you've pulled a number of the markers out of the box at the same time, chances are excellent that the rest of them will just fall down on their sides, requiring you to shake them out of the box.  To save myself the hassle, I found a conveniently-sized plastic storage container (the disposable ones you can get at the grocery store, or dollar store), and the markers are all now happily living in there.  I like that it has a cover, too.  You do need to be careful to close the caps firmly on the markers (just like all markers), so your paint doesn't dry up.  Time will tell how durable these markers are; but at $14.99 for 24 markers (as of this writing), I won't feel badly about just replacing them when the time comes.

Content: Overall these are good paint markers. Especially if you plan to use them on porous materials like paper, canvases, or shoes. I have used them on a few non porous surfaces (like laptops, tablet cases, and phone cases) and I didn't like how you could not go back over a color (say if you missed a spot or wanted a 2nd coat) until it fully dried which took a couple minutes to do so. I have used other paint markers where I did not have this problem. This is the ONLY reason I gave them 4 stars instead of 5. I know that a couple minutes isn't a lot of time but those minutes add up. Especially when you are trying to work on and finish a project for someone else in a timely manner. I like that they are dual tipped and how they don't have to be primed before using. They aren't messy and I don't feel I will have any issue with them leaking. The colors are pretty but like with some other markers the color doesn't always match the color on the cap. I put each color on a piece of white and black card stock paper and then used a black sharpie to number them so I would roughly know how that color would appear when I use them. I did notice though that some markers appear slightly different depending on what tip you use. Some colors (mainly the lighter colors) also appear differently depending on the color you are applying them on but I think that is expected. On non porous materials (like laptops, tablet cases, and phone cases) you can test out a small area though to see how the color will look. Just wipe it off quicly. Overall, they are good paint markers especially for smaller and more basic projects. I think these would be GREAT to use for younger kids since you don't have to prime them and they aren't messy. Hope this helps someone who is on the fence about buying these.

Content:
I've tried several different paint pens for rock painting, and so far these are my absolute favorite.

The colors are lovely and the size of the pen tip is perfect for most of my needs (I do use other pens for wide areas, and a Sharpie pen for very thin lines). I haven't had any issues with dryness, and I've only had one leak but I think it may have been my fault (not sure exactly what happened but it didn't leak again after I wiped it down and took the lid off and put it on again).

The paint itself seems to be pretty decent quality - it goes down smoothly, dries decently quickly (I do paint 3-5 rocks at a time though to accommodate drying time), and it's really good at allowing layers. I've made many a mistake (not the steadiest hand), and was able to fix them easily enough. It even goes over Sharpie okay, though that does take a few more layers than just over other paint colors.

I'm seriously in love with these paint pens - I wouldn't have been able to paint an awesome Rick Sanchez over a portal background without them.

1000000% recommend these!!!

Content: I used these acrylic pens to paint rocks. It was my first time painting rocks so I was unsure what products to buy. I first used acrylic paint and brushes for the background on my rocks. After they dried, I used these pens for the details and all the writing. Overall they were great. I can have a shaky hand and inconsistent handwriting on paper but I think most of the handwriting came out pretty good on the rocks. Every once in awhile, if the rocks had a little dip or crack or something in it, the marker would catch and mess up my writing. I'd just paint over it and wait for it to dry then try again. Luckily this didn't happen very often. Think that's more of a rock painting issue though, not a problem with the product. When writing, I learned to write very slowly. If you go to fast the tip will sling paint. If you go slow, you'll have a much better result. I did notice sometimes the pens would appear to dry out as others noted in reviews, but with a few shakes or some pressure on the tip, I've been able to get the pens to start working perfectly again in no time. I've painted over 100 rocks (some a few times - when i didn't like something about my first try 😅) and all of the pens are still fully functioning and seem to have plenty of paint left. The white pen, which is one of the ones I've used the most, has started to crack a little on the tip (see picture). I think it may just be because I'm writing on uneven rocks though. If I don't pay attention, the cracked tip makes the handwriting very bad as it causes the paint to come out inconsistently. I just make sure to tilt the white pen a certain angle and it works just as it did when I first bought it. I do wish the pens differentiated between the finer and medium point tips. I threw them all in one box and the pens have no markings to indicate if they're fine point or not. Luckily, both tips seem to work fine for what I'm using them for. There's not a huge difference between the two but it would be nice to know. Overall, great pens. Definitely recommend!

Content: I call these "generic Chinese pens" because the box and pens don't have a company/brand name on them, and I've seen the same set for sale on Amazon under at least 2 different company names. If you're going to buy them search Amazon and buy the least expensive - you'll know they're the same because of the box design and the lettering on the pens.  The quality is pretty average for this type of pen.The instructions on the included 'instruction manual' say to shake them at least 30 times before using and I found out why - if you don't mix them thoroughly before each use you can end up with watery thin paint, or tiny clumps of paint. The description calls them 'extra-fine' - I'd  call it medium fine but they do make good lines.  In my opinion the color selection is just OK - I'd like to have a brighter green and blue than these. I did a swatch chart so you can judge for yourself, but note the colors are not numbered or named on the pens or caps, and the cap color is only a general indication of the paint color.  I couldn't get the colors to blend well either when they were both wet, or by overlaying one color on another dry color.  The colors do show up pretty well on black paper which is a plus to me (see the doodle I uploaded). On the down side these seem to be very wet paints even when thoroughly mixed and they do bleed through thin paper.  I haven't used them on rocks, plastic or ceramics but I suspect they would be better suited for those materials.  If you do use paper you'll probably want to use a heavier weight (like for watercolors or mixed media).  Because of the wetness they take a bit longer to dry than other acrylic pens I've used.Important: You'll need to prime these after mixing before the first use - quickly press the tip straight down on some scrap material and release - you'll see the nib (tip) fill with paint.  I'd recommend using cardboard as there's a good chance of ending up with a puddle or drips.  Also I'd recommend doing a line on scrap paper before actually using to remove any excess paint from the nib.  The instructions say if one gets clogged you can remove the nib and wash it out with warm water, but I'm not going to try that as it would undoubtedly make a mess.  I have yet to use these where I didn't end up with a little paint on my hand.  As far as storage, the box isn't going to last long - if you do buy these I'd recommend keeping them in a cheap pencil case (there are plenty on Amazon).  All in all these are OK pens for casual use at the current price, but if you want professional quality definitely look elsewhere.

Content: These acrylic paint markers really did impress me with their quality and the amount of colors you receive for the price. The value for your money is very good and these are quite nice. I like the range of colors that it contains and the box that it comes in is pretty good for storage too. It opens from the top and has a flat bottom so it stands up and you can easily swap markers out without having to close it up and open it up each time while you are in the middle of a project. These paint pens also are super quick to get started and flowing in comparison to other brands that I have tried. These take maybe 2-4 seconds to start up and get the color going when you use it for the first time which is so fast and not a hassle at all. As for the flow and saturation of the markers, I am very pleased. They are highly pigmented colors and not transparent. They make nice solid color that dries rather fast so you can easily layer another color over the top without worrying about smudges. It also seems line you don’t have to really do a ton of coats to get a nice solid streak free color, but I haven’t tried it on a ton of different materials yet so this is still up for review. I also really like the size of the nib that these come with. I am not a fan of paint pens with a very fine tip as they tend to get clogged up quickly snd I just don’t think that I usually want a fine tip when I am looking to use a paint pen. I am usually looking to cover a larger area or a material that is not traditional paper so a broader tip is usually the way I achieve what I am wanting with a paint pen and these markers are the perfect size. Overall, I think these are super awesome quality for the price and I may switch to these for my main paint markers from a more expensive brand that are my go to. These are just as good, if not better in some aspects. These are great for any level of artist from beginner to professional, and I think this set would be great for gifting as well.

Content:
Very much like Poscas. Some of the colors look identical, in fact, including one of the yellows, the light green, the red, and the black and white. The blues and purples are different. They seem to pump/fill a bit faster than Poscas, although they are extremely similar at a much more reasonable price point. The yellows seemed a bit more opaque. Same factory maybe?? Required little shaking to get them started compared to other markers I've used. Love them. Wish they had more colors and other sizes/nibs.

UPDATE: I bought the new 36 set and the paint seemed a bit thinner. There is a nice range of blues and purples, although they could've varied the tones (or even the hues) of the purples. Same for the yellows. When overlapping to fill a larger area, the sheen is a bit different ranging from matte to satin.

I need to compare these to the first set I got. Several colors are like Poscas, but they have unique colors not available in the Posca line, including the yellows and the cool greens. One criticism of this set is that except for the really light green, they are all blue-leaning greens. This set needs one or two warm greens. An emerald or middle-of-the road green.

It seems like the selection of colors was intentional in the way they filled in the missing Posca colors, but also careless as they should have spent more time tweaking the colors. The oranges have a lot of white in them. Similar to Posca, but too much white. This is just one example of where they needed to put forth more time before releasing a product.

Definitely the sheen, film of these markers is different from Posca. Posca's are all matte (you can feel the roughness). It took a lot of chemistry to develop this as every pigment has its own sheen (yes, some pigments are glossy and need added agents to make them more matte).

One of the markers released liquid orange paint that flew through the air when I used it (and landed on my table). These definitely seem more liquid than the other sets I bought. So, nitpicking aside, I like these.

They work well with Poscas and are very similar except not quite as matte or consistently matte. As a standalone set, the greens are lacking in hues. But for the money you pay, they're a nice addition to a marker collection.

The listing now says they are lightfast. I am going to test them, as Posca reds, pinks, browns (and probably purples) fade a lot, and the lightfast ones available from other companies don't perform as well as these or Poscas as Liquitex and Amsterdam have not perfected their paint formulas (they have been selling markers long enough to make them better quality also).

Being lightfast is huge, if, in fact they are, and it would be nice to see this company share how they were tested--or include lightfast ratings. One other marker dealer, Tooli-Art claims to be lightfast, but the proof is in the pudding, and when companies don't rate the lightfastness or the testing standards, it doesn't lend a lot of credibility to the claims, but let's hope this, that SFAIH is telling the truth and their reds, pinks, and purples are really lightfast, which makes them truly artist grade...

After using these, I was able, after letting them dry for a couple weeks, to use a brush-on, Liquitex matte varnish full strength, no fussing. Note, I was able to do this with Poscas too. The key is to let the paint sit for a length of time, not try to do it the same day or even the next day because they will bleed if the paint has not cured. One you use a matte or other varnish, the discrepancies in finish disappear.

One more feature to mention, these have numbers available on the ends for your charts. Will they be sold open stock? Would be lovely to see these in small nib sizes with nib replacements (I am wondering if they will take Posca nibs)... Great Buy.

Content:
These markers are great FUN! And, yes, they actually deliver OPAQUE ACRYLIC PAINT. I had never heard of such a thing before ordering this set.

The markers are simple to use. You press down to start the paint flowing, and the more you press the marker down or the longer you press, the more paint flows down the nib. Hence you can make somewhat wider or thinner lines, even though the range is limited. The lines themselves are uniform, and the flow is consistent.

The paints adhere very well, as you would expect from acrylic paint. They dried quickly and the colors remained beautifully vibrant (see pic).

The paints are quite opaque on white, but might need a second coat on a dark substrate. (see pic)

I've found them perfect for outlining large shapes, and mistakes can be cleaned up with a q-tip and water before they dry.

They are useful for rock painting and can be used for 'dotting', the dots from them are beautifully round. You can also paint on glass, plastic, wood, etc. with them.

One last thing I'd like to mention: I would love to see these markers with a range of different sizes of nibs, if that's possible. I had to use a fine sharpie, not the acrylic markers, for the fine purple lines in the hair on my picture.

CONCLUSION: For the current price of $18.99, I believe these pens are a really great value. I've had a blast using them.

In terms of negatives the only thing we can comment on now is the size of the points which are 2-3mm in diameter. This is a medium sized point that is really good for filling and broad coverage. For work on 2-3" diameter rocks, we wish these points were a little finer.

These marker pens are well made and meet the descriptions and images shown on the website. The paint pens work very well and provide very good first coat coverage. Better than some well-known more expensive brands. We're very happy to have them and would recommend them to friends and family. We feel these pens are a bargain.

Content: I bought these for painting presentation and auction pieces only to find that color is inconsistent.I got different shades of the color while using a single color. The color doesn't perfectly match stroke-by-stroke.It appears that the pigments separate in the barrel, so as the paint flows it changes in tone, which makes it extremely difficult to get even color. I have even experienced severe whitening and darkening of the single hue to the point of consideration. I have ended up going several times over certain areas of my painting to get the color to even out or at least blend with itself satisfactorily.I have used many acrylic paint markers and these don't particularly stand out to me as a superior marker, actually I found them to be more satisfying to paint with, but less satisfying in end result because of the pigment separation. Because of the separation of pigments my strokes became bothersome and aggravating, and it actually became difficult to match the colors to themselves when trying to cover larger areas. All of the bad experiences I had with color separation happened while using the brush end of the markers, which allows for more flow.There is a wide array of colors, which is nice. The paints do flow well, they cover ok, sometimes they are opaque and sometimes they are semi-transparent... especially when painting over white or black (particularly black shows through other colors quite well requiring several coats to cover thoroughly.)I did find that the fine tip end is pretty good for lining, and similar to a calligraphy nib, you can adjust your pressure to get thicker/thinner lines.These are ok, for practice maybe, but I wouldn't be depending on these for a go to marker for literal presentation pieces.I can suggest these for kids, for practice, or just general crafting/ coloring use. I would not suggest them for presentation artwork, fine application, or any application where consistency and quality are a key factor.I gave the item three stars because of the disappointing color separation.I do suggest this item with heed to application needs.

Content: I have no experience with acrylic markers. Acrylic paint yes and markers of various types yes, but not this style, but I wanted to try them out since I collect various art supplies. I hoped they would behave like overly large gel pens and give me the ability to add some details over black ink or black paint, and they do that, but there is more going on. For instance I used one to write on the lid of a jar of pigment to label it, no smudging once it was dry which was excellent.Mostly I tested these on mixed media paper, some of the fine point sides were a little dried out and required wiping off before they would work. It was a learning experience, my silly illustration turned out a lot more pop art since you layer rather than shade in a gradient to get dimension (in contrast with the alcohol markers which can give you a softer edge, these want a much more harsh distinct lines) these are really not the style I usually work with, but since they are waterproof (I did an ink wash over the whole piece once dried) I could do some really fun mixed media pieces with ink and paint. There is little to no smell and they dry fairly quickly, since they can go on multiple surfaces I find myself wondering if I can add an interesting mural to the side of my boring black computer desk. I am glad I got these markers and look forward to integrating them more in my art and seeing what other weird things I can do with them.

Content: I'm a multimedia artist for both the eyes and the ears, and I've been looking for my voice while making my own album covers. Content: I ordered these for my wife who paints rocks as a hobby.In this hobby my wife uses a combination of paint markers and paint brushes along with small containers of paint.The paint markers are very convenient, but they can struggle when it comes to extremes:  fine lines and covering large areas. These particular marker set was chosen mainly for their broad tip coverage.The felt tip on these markers has a flat form that is rectangular in shape.  The rectangular shape is wide but narrow and the narrow ends are cut sharply so you can use the sharpened edge for fine lines. But for my wife we were mostly interested in using the broadest aspect of the tip to replace the use of a board brush. Using the markers makes it simpler to change colors and simpler to clean up. More time doing the creating vs. prepping.As a test we selected 2 rocks. One had been previously painted with yellow and one that was bare. We were testing for coverage and drying time.We painted the yellow rock with blue, which by the way is a very pretty shade of blue. The paint went on thick and wet and for us took 5 minutes or so to dry. Once dry the color was more of a mat finish than glossy but the blue covered the yellow completely.We then painted the bare rock with white. Truthfully, this was not a dark color rock, but it represented a typical grayish rock that we commonly use. Again, the white went on smoothly, thick and wet. Really no problems. The broad brush covered the 3" diameter flat rock in a very short time - as we hoped. Drying was again in around 5 minutes or so. At that point we were able to paint over the white with the blue marker.So, these brushes worked as we expected. We'll be trying them now painting background colors and large expanses. This work will test how long the tip lasts, determining if they leak or leave blobs and do the paint markers have enough paint capacity to be cost effective compared to brushes and paint. But for now, we're happy with what we've received. The cost is reasonable especially if they have good capacity. It's really nice to be able to grab markers for this part of the work. It definitely shortens up the time getting paints and paint brushes ready and then there is the cleaning aspect. So, these markers were a nice addition to our kit. If you've had the same experiences, we think these are worth the try.

Content: The product is good, dries quickly and will work well for my needs, for the most part. The description is a bit confusing though. It indicates that you have three width options, from fairly fine to thick (2-3 mm to 15 mm). It also says that the nib is 2-sided. I thought that perhaps the different ends of the nib would have different widths so that it would be fairly easy to get the fine-medium-thick lines but that's not the case. The nib is the same on both ends and you need to play around with the marker to figure out how to get the width you want. The widest is easy, but apparently each side of the nib is cut with slightly different angles so tilting it one way gives you the medium width line and tilting it the other way or rotating the pen will give you the finest line. You can't do real detailed work with this, at least not that I can see. Maybe with a lot of practice. I do think there is a good value to the wider lines but will have to get a fine nibbed pen to do the more detailed work I need this for.

Content: I use wide tipped markers when labeling boxes so that I can easily see what's inside from several feet away.  In fact, I use them for labeling just about everything!  The problem with most permanent markers (at least for me) is that the ink simply dries out too fast.  I can't speak to the longevity of the BIGTHUMB markers because I haven't owned them long or used them a lot but if they end up having an even shorter life than the other markers, I will be back to update this review.  For now, I'm going to assume that they have a reasonably long life and I hope that turns out to be the case because I'm delighted with the way they mark.  Because they are paint markers, once the ink is flowing you get great coverage and have the option of making very wide to thin marks with a single stroke. I suppose the life of the marker will also greatly depend upon the size stroke you make with it; for my purposes, the medium to smaller tip is perfect.  The one caution I would give is that they do take a bit longer to dry than regular permanent markers because the pens are dispensing acrylic paint rather than ink.  Marks are still relatively quick drying but not instant drying so take a bit of extra care, particularly when the markers are first used, so that you don't smudge your work or end up with paint all over yourself!

Content: I've never used Posca markers before, but having recently entered the adult coloring community, I have heard others sing their praises, and now I can say, rightfully so. So there's that.  But the markers themselves are kind of impressive for what they are.  The paint/ink is smooth.  It comes easily off the tip with streaking or skipping.  The color is bright and yet opaque.  I just wrote some words with the colors on marker paper and was extremely surprised by the quality.However, my one "concern" is that the markers themselves feel rather light, which makes me wonder exactly how much paint/ink is in them and how long I can expect them to last before I need to replace them.  Posca markers not cheap.  They are at the highest end of paint makers in the field.  Please see the 62 ct set in this listing if you are unsure of what that means.  I guess I just want to know that I'm getting my money's worth at the price point.  I also think that I would have preferred to have this set with more colors at the same size for the price rather repeating the 11 colors just to have two different sizes.  But overall, this is a quality set.  NOW I GET IT.

Content:
I use markers for a variety of crafts, and have purchased way too many glitter, metallic and other specialty markers online and from local craft stores.

WHAT MAKES THIS A GOOD SET:
First, that you get so many different styles of markers in one big box that's easy to store. Anyone that has priced buying these in small sets or even individually will appreciate that.
The glitter pens are pretty glittery. I have a few glitter pens that are a different brand that are more glittery, but they were expensive pens that I had to buy individually from a local craft store. For the price of these, the glitter effect is pretty good.
The metallic markers are also pretty good. The effect is comparable to other brands I have that cost slightly more than these.
You get a good variety of colors in the Classic, Pastel, Neon, Morandi (which are "muted" colors btw, vs bright neon colors). The white, and other light-colored markers do a great job - bright and easy to see on dark paper.

THINGS TO KEEP IN MIND:
When you want to use one of these markers, you kinda have to "get them flowing" initially. They printed a little diagram on the side showing you how to pump them to get them flowing. If you're not getting a very strong, bold line, you need to pump the marker some more, to get the ink flowing better.
Due to the nature of how ink flows from these markers, you can get the best result using them if you're very purposeful in your marks. If you want to make quick, very fast marks, these may not be the pens for you.

- My biggest complaint is the box they come in. The way that this box is depicted in the product description pictures makes it seem like it arrives in a tiered, organized box. It's just a box. It's a nice box, but it's just a box, without any tiers or dividers. The markers themselves are numbered, and the back of the box has a chart or "key" that you can use, to identify what type of marker each number is.
Additionally, the names of the actual colors are not on the box, nor are they on the markers themselves. This might not bother you, but for colorblind folks like myself, not having the actual name of the color written on these markers can be a bit of an issue.

Overall, this is a good variety of specialty markers that I'm sure to get a lot of use out of.

Content: The only reason why I’m rating these markers three out of five stars is because of the size. They are extremely small and have thin barrels. Personally, I feel like there is not a lot of paint in them and I can see them running out really fast if you use them consistently. I wish the packaging and came in was more sturdy and not the flimsy plastic. Reminds me a pack of markers you would get at the dollar tree. I love how it comes with the booklet of paper and two different swatch sheets. The pigment from the markers are really nice and they dry matte. I love the metallics they are so pretty. For a beginner artist or a child I feel like these are great to have to learn the basics. However, If you are an intermediate or professional artist, I would suggest the Posca paint pens over these because they have more paint in them and will not run out as fast. I’m not saying you can’t make great artwork with these. You don’t need expensive art supplies to create great work but they have a beginner feel to them. Also another downside is that if you run out of one color, you would possibly have to rebuy a pack to get the color than buying it individually. Overall they’re good but not great. I’m not head over and heels with love with them.

Content: Instead of having a traditional guestbook at my wedding, I decided to have a sign to put up along with wedding pictures, for our guests to write their messages on.I got a wood sign, in gray. I didn’t want people to write all over it in black sharpie, since this sign will be part of my home decor, I don’t want black sharpie writing displayed on my living room wall. I decided that white writing would look nicest against the gray background.I came across these paint pens. I liked the idea of using permanent acrylic paint instead of ink. I also liked that these were extra fine tip, which would make writing easier.I tested them out as soon as I got them, because I wanted to know if they’d be any good, or if I’d need to get different ones. I had a piece of scrap wood that was close to being the same gray as the sign. The directions said that before using them the first time, to press the tip down a couple of times to get the paint to flow down to the tip of the pen. I did that with both pens a couple times on my scrap wood, until each one left a circle of paint. I tested writing with each pen, and they were super easy to write with. The flow of the paint was nice and steady, and consistent.The wedding was a few weeks later. We were outdoors, in 104 degrees. Both pens continued to work perfectly. No chunky blotches, no drips, and no smearing. I posted a photo of how the sign that was written on with these pens, but the pic honestly doesn’t do it justice. In person, the white paint is a little more vibrant and bright. To put it simply, the white POPS!

Content: I love the Sharpie brand, use them all the time, but had never seen these.  I didn't read closely and thought they were liquid chalk pens, which show up well on acrylic boards I use on my refrigerator for calendar events and notes.  So I rush to test them out, and wow!  They show up bright and clear on a stainless steel refrigerator background, a white background, and an almond background.  Regular acrylic markers don't really work well on these acrylic boards at all. Liquid pens do the job but prefer a white background.  So I backed my magnetic refrigerator acrylic boards with white foam board and I was in business.  You can see in the photos how easy it is to read the Sharpie writing against the various backgrounds.My first test I wrote on the board and immediately wiped with water.  No problem.  But then after I was in ecstacy at the Sharpie performance I went back to erase and water didn't do the trick.  Because these are not liquid chalk pens, they are special acrylic pens.  I tried two or three cleaners and could erase the writing but only with some elbow grease.  Then I used plain alcohol, and voila!  Clean wipes immediately.Of course this is not the main purpose of these Sharpies, but now that I know how to use them I may eventually remove my white foam boards and just use the Sharpies got my magnetic acrylic boards.  It probably depends on how much trouble I have with the liquid chalk markers.The real claim to fame is the artistry you can achieve on glass, metal, any surface really with the Sharpies.  I suspect there isn't another product out there that will do as good a job.  Sharpe does it again!!!!

Content: My family uses acrylic paint markers for a variety of reasons, and I've never really found a brand that I love--they tend to bleed through, some can't layer without becoming muddy, and priming them is annoying as they tend to have an abrupt splotch/blot of color. I was really excited to get a chance to test this acrylic marker from Sharpie out as they claim to layer well, not bleed through, and not need priming, so thank you to the Stellar Product Testing Panel for giving me these Sharpie Acrylic Creative Markers to try! I'll cut to the chase: I found them to be exactly as advertised. I loved them so much in the 5 pack I received to test that I immediately went and ordered the 12 pack they also have available after I tried them out.They didn't bleed through on any of the papers I tried (standard printer, card stock, glossy papers, etc.), and could layer on top of other colors when dry. They dried very quickly on everything except for the glossy/slick materials--even on these they didn't have a long dry time and didn't budge once dried. Even on dark paper the Sharpie Acrylic Creative Markers were bright, bold, and clear. I cannot overstate how much I loved that they didn't need priming--anyone who uses paint markers has probably had the misfortune to have a blotch of paint come out when priming, but the Sharpie Acrylic Markers didn't have that problem at all. I loved that.Finally, they cleaned off of my skin with basic soap, water, and a bit of handwashing. No problem at all! I'm very happy with them and will be a customer going forward

Content: At about $11.00 or 46 cents per marker these double-ended acrylic markers seem to be a really good value for the money.  I don't have much experience with acrylic markers so I was happy to see that I could try them out for not a whole lot of money, in case I decided that I don't like working with acrylic paint.  I was interested in using them on canvas and they are advertised as being for painting on "multi-surface" - paper, canvas, glass, cermaci and stone.  I like the way the color/paint flows easily and evenly - one or two coats needed at the most.  The colors don't bleed through canvas or "standard/regular" paper which is really nice and actually surprised me.  As far as the colors themselves, the red is really more of a pink than a red but for the most part the colors match what you see on the box.  Most of the colors are opaque  and there are a few metallic colors.  I couldn't really see much of a difference between the two tips - brush vs dot, except when I wanted to paint dots - then it was clear that there is a difference.  But, if not painting "dots" there is really little difference between the two tips.  I tried painting on glass and stone; the paint glided on very easily but took awhile to completely dry - reminded me of how you have to wait for nail polish to dry completely.  Since this is a water based ink I imagine that if you got water on whatever you are painting with these markers, the paint will run and dissolve.  For someone wondering if they would like to paint with acrylic markers, I think this is a nice little starter set for not a whole lot of money.

Content:
Purchased the set of 24 (came in a blue box) - wanted more than just basic colors but didn't want to spend a lot - a good compromise. Haven't used these yet except to test them out, but so far, so good. Pros: 1) they write nice - nice flow, movement, etc. 2) as 'paint' pens, there's no shaking or pressing to get the paint to flow. 3_ The pens I received all seem to be 'full' with no dried out tips - I tested both ends of each pen. 4) The lids all have a nice 'snap' and stay on securely. Cons: 1) The box comes with a swatch on the back, giving each color a name and number - but the pens themselves have neither names or numbers, so you can ONLY go by the lid color. And that's pretty tricky. While testing, I made a mark on the swatch with the best, to me, corresponding colored pen. Some colors are amazingly close, others - not at all. First photo shows how I -mistakenly- marked the 'brown' pen on 'Gingerbread' before realizing it left no swatch for the lighter (tan) color. Yeah - the 'brown' is supposed to be 'Stone Grey' apparently. Go figure. In a case like this, I like to mark the pen on a white label, cut a strip, and stick it around the lid of the pen so I can see the true color. Unfortunately, 2) the lids are all very textured with ridges, so this time I'll have to stick it on the pen itself. But where? not on either end close to the caps (it'd cover the symbol showing which tip is which, & don't want it under my fingers when using the pens) so it'll have to go in the center of pen, annoyingly over the text. Not really any other option.
Overall, I do like the pens and would buy them again - the annoyances are small compared to their quality.
Edit: Added my 'actual color' strip to each pen (except black, white, gold, & silver) and added the color # in case I decide to order a larger variety later. Amazingly, the actual colors are VERY close to the cap colors! Amazing because this isn't usually the case! The photo shows how just 2 of the colors are a bit off - the bright pink & the yellow next to it in the top row. Realized I missed the 'tan' and 'grey' pens after the photo was taken. The tan is spot on, but the grey ... it's the same color as the cap, but lighter. You'd need 2-3 coats to make it the same as the cap.
As for how they work - great! Coverage, even over a dark color, is impressive. On the head shown I used black (for the outlines and the eye area), red, light & dark blue, and white (ONLY for the dots on the black part of the eye). The light blue was over the black of the eye and 2-3 coats gave the color shown.

Content:
For the price, these are excellent paint pens. They function about how you'd expect - they're lightweight so easy to hold, they have quite vibrant colors, and they will work on many surface types. I'm using them on a light, unstained wood, and I have to use at least two coats of whatever color I'm using. That being said, the end product is going to look really nice.

The case they come in is not the best, so I would recommend planning for an alternate storage solution. I purchased a separate pen/pencil case for them that will hold them horizontally as is recommended from the product for how to store them.

The fine side writes really fine and nice. The thicker side is all good. If you go in swirls, you can't really see the strokes. That said, I go side to side because I like the look of strokes because it really screams hand painted. You will need to leave whatever project it is to sit and dry. It's still paint, and as such needs to dry. If you grab it right after, you will get paint on yourself. Thus, if you're getting these for children, I would recommend close supervision. Otherwise, I can see people of most ages really enjoying these for art projects, and especially those who may find it difficult to hold certain brushes or those who don't have storage space for lots of brush types, palettes, etc. Paint pens are a nice alternative.

You can paint over your mistakes after they've dried. I have tested that because I don't have the steadiest hand, so I make mistakes often. However, I have not tried to correct a lighter color over a darker color. Only dark over light, so be mindful that it's paint. It will bleed or blend together. Would not recommend for single-use/one-day projects. Most projects with these will need multiple days. I could see this being fun for really unique beading designs if you're making household decor, crafts, jewelry, etc.

Content: I use paint markers to paint rocks.Here's what these are like:Colors: The colors are extremely close, if not exact matches to the marker caps. This is important because on some markers the colors are very different than their caps and when you're making art you want to know what the paint actually looks like.Paint quality: Thin, dries quickly and is very translucent. It takes 5+ coats to cover a surface. One of the biggest problems with these markers is that the colors mix when you layer them. For example, if you paint down green, and then let it dry completely, and then paint white over it it, your white marker will be ruined and pick up the green paint. My other acrylic markers don't do that.Tips: The brush tip is great as a brush. It' makes it easy to do thin lines and also fill in large areas quickly. I do like that you don't have to press the tips to release paint, although sometimes this is frustrating when you want the paint to go on thickly or in more quantity.Overall - Good for kids and teens. Probably best for paper. Not at all appropriate for serious artists.

Content:
First time using paint pens of any kind, so take this review with a grain of salt ofc!!

Was apprehensive about buying something like Posca pens because of the price and not knowing whether or not I’d actually enjoy them, so I decided to try these as like a…trial run I guess.

PROS:

Firstly, they are super easy to use. I particularly like the brush nib because it allows for that line variation and filling in larger areas.
Something to note is that I’m using suuuuuper thin (A5) paper, and so far, after layer upon layer—the paper hasn’t buckled hardly at all!! Was a really nice surprise tbh!! In fact, the only thing that made it buckle and bleed through was the pen I was using for my lines after laying down the paint. I have been having so much fun experimenting with the colors (which there are a lot!!)

CONS:

Be prepared to layer these. They aren’t suuuuper duper pigmented like others I’ve seen especially if you’re laying a light color over a dark one, even after shaking them for a bit as it says to do on the back of the box. (Though in all honesty, I enjoy it more as a feature than a con, but I know some people might not find that appealing—but it could be that I’m impatient and don’t shake them long enough before use)
Something I also noticed is that there are NO lighter/pastel type colors. It’s not a huge deal, but I’d really love a few of those just to lighten things up if I need to. Generally good flow, but some of the markers have little fibers on the nib that need to be picked off. ALSO. Before you start layering, give the first layer a little bit of time to dry. I noticed it takes about 10 seconds but then you’re good to go!!

I will say though, for the price and what you get, they work wonderfully and other than what I listed above I can’t think of any complaints!! Great for anyone like me who hasn’t tried them before and doesn’t wanna break the bank on other brands. :)

Content: This set of 80 acrylic paint pens earns a mixed review.  The pens are neatly packaged in a sturdy and organized zipper case.  This makes storing the pens horizontally easy and ensures your art area is not messy.  I laid out the case and took a piece of pre-cut 4X6-inch white cardstock.  I attempted to start drawing with the black pen.  I couldn’t get the cap off the paint pen.  I eventually had to get a rubber gripper that is used to remove jar lids.  I got into a rhythm and was soon able to remove the tops off the sample pens I tried as I drew my drawing.  I needed to twist and pull using the rubber gripping pad.  If you have arthritis, you may have to work around the fact that the tops are incredibly difficult to get off the paint pens.I started with the black pen, creating a basic drawing to fill in with different colors.  First, I used traditional paint markers to fill in the petals of the flowers.  Then, I used several metallic markers to fill in the flower center and leaves.  Finally, I touched up the black ink and attempted to do some detail work.  I colored the four blue corners last.  The three white dots in those corners took three coats with the white acrylic paint marker.  In contrast, the whitish/grey coloring on the stems is one coat with the white marker (see photograph).The paint pens dry fairly quickly.  I got several paint spots on my hands, which I cleaned with a scrub brush, warm water, and hand soap.  The black pen easily covered minimal mistakes made while coloring the petals and center.  I had to use a light touch, or the nib would wear away my paper. I used a metallic pen to color the center of the flowers. The paint flow was too heavy and made a mess when I opened it.  Eventually, that particular marker’s paint flow slowed, and I could continue to use it.I decided to test whether these paint pens are waterproof and quick-drying.  I waited fifteen minutes after I was done with the drawing.  I wetted down a paper towel with three squirts of water and dragged it two times across the right-hand side of the drawing.  The ink did not smear on the paper but lifted off and covered my paper towel (see photograph).  I have concerns about using these paint pens on anything exposed to water.  Paint from both the regular and metallic pens was present on the paper towel.On another 4X6-inch piece of cardstock, I used two colors to write letters, numbers, and common words  (see photograph).  As you can see, the medium-sized nibs make detailed drawing and writing difficult.  The manufacturer does not hide this; few examples of tiny writing or detailing are on the product description page.  Additional acrylic pens to finish your artwork may be necessary, depending on what you are creating.This paint pen set is much better than others I have tried, but it misses the mark with caps that can’t be easily removed and paint that is not waterproof.  Even with that in mind, I believe this is still a good value for 80-paint pens.  This set may work for you if you are a doodler and want to have fun.  However, if you are serious about your art, you may need to look elsewhere to be completely satisfied.

Content: I drew a small drawing of flowers, testing several paint markers from this kit.  The acrylic paint markers work well on paper.  There is good paint flow without excess paint on the paper.  I had excellent control of paint placement.  Also, the markers did not require any shaking.  The large selection of colors is pleasing.  I let the drawing set for fifteen minutes.  The manufacturer claims these markers are fast-drying and waterproof.  I ran my fingers across the paper’s surface without ink on my fingers.  Next, I wet down a paper towel with a spray bottle.  I rubbed it a few times across the drawing.  (See the result in the photographs.)  These acrylic paint markers are not waterproof.  There is a minor smearing of paint on the paper, and a great deal of paint came off on the paper towel.  This is disappointing and will affect how I can use these markers.  If you plan on using them with any medium exposed to water, you should probably look elsewhere for acrylic paint markers.  I used a lead test swab on the paint in my drawing.  It appears to be lead-free.  I would give these acrylic paint pens more than two stars had the pens been waterproof.  The fact that they are not limits their usefulness.

Content: I love using acrylic paint pens for my art and i jumped on ordering these thinking they would be dual tipped (diff size nibs) of the same color. UNFORTUNATELY, THAT’S NOT THE CASE HERE.Here’s what you get:- 50 paint pens that are dual tipped, BUT there’s 2 different colors on each pen. For example, Black on one side, white on the other. While I appreciate a 100 color palette, why not just make the product a 100 pack of colors that have a fine/brush tip for each color. Ex: White (brush/fine tip), not a diff color on the end. What if I want or need a brush tip of black to put in a large coverage spot and i only have it as a fine tip nib? That’s going to use up the black most likely and be time consuming.- Because of there being 2 diff colors on the dual tips, the case they come in is absolutely useless. If you are someone who likes to see their color palette so you know what to use, you will need to dump these out into a transparent case so you can see them as the box is not see-thru. Unless you don’t mind fishing around and searching for 5-10min to find your color, then by all means, leave them in their box.Their saving grace is that they can blend. While they don’t blend the best compared to others I’ve used, they’re certainly not the worst at it. They can and will blend, you just have to be fast about it. They also can be used on a variety of surfaces.If my identified cons don’t bother you, then this will be a good set for you. If you’re like me and like to see your colors, just dump these out into a case or the surface you’re working on.
